These algorithms use simple _selection policies_ to chose next action to play in each decision point based on statistics of rewards achieved after individual actions. We study whether Hannan consistency of the selection policies is sufficient to guarantee convergence of SM-MCTS to a Nash equilibrium of the game. We also investigate whether a similar relation holds between the approximate versions of Hannan consistency and Nash equilibria.
In Theorem [4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 4.1. ‣ 4 Insufficiency of Local Regret Minimization for Global Convergence ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"), we prove a negative result, which is in our opinion the most surprising and interesting part of the paper, which is the fact that Hannan consistency alone does not guarantee a good performance of the standard SM-MCTS. We present a Hannan consistent selection policy that causes SM-MCTS to converge to a solution far from the equilibrium.
We show that this could be avoided by a slight modification to SM-MCTS (which we call SM-MCTS-A), which updates the selection policies by the average reward obtained after a joined action of both players in past simulations, instead of the result of the current simulation.
In Theorem [5.4](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S5.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 5.4. ‣ 5.1 Asymptotic convergence of SM-MCTS-A ‣ 5 Convergence of SM-MCTS and SM-MCTS-A ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"), we prove that SM-MCTS-A combined with any Hannan consistent (resp. approximately HC) selection policy with guaranteed exploration converges to a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium (resp. an approximate subgame-perfect NE) in this class of games.
For selection policies which are only approximately HC, we present bounds on the eventual distance from a Nash equilibrium.
In Theorem [5.12](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S5.Thmtheorem12 "Theorem 5.12. ‣ 5.2.2 The convergence of SM-MCTS ‣ 5.2 Asymptotic convergence of SM-MCTS ‣ 5 Convergence of SM-MCTS and SM-MCTS-A ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"), we show that under additional assumptions on the selection policy, even the standard SM-MCTS can guarantee the convergence. We do this by defining the property of having unbiased payoff observations (UPO), and showing that it is a sufficient condition for the convergence.
We then empirically confirm that the two commonly used Hannan consistent algorithms, Exp3 and regret matching, satisfy this property, thus justifying their use in practice.
We further investigate the empirical speed of convergence and show that the eventual distance from the equilibrium is typically much better than the presented theoretical guarantees.
We empirically show that SM-MCTS generally converges as close to the equilibrium as SM-MCTS-A, but does it faster.
Finally, we give theoretical grounds for some practical improvements, which may be used with SM-MCTS, but have not been formally justified. These include removal of exploration samples from the resulting strategy and the use of average strategy instead of empirical frequencies of action choices.
All presented theoretical results trivially apply also to perfect information games with sequential moves. The counterexample in Theorem [4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 4.1. ‣ 4 Insufficiency of Local Regret Minimization for Global Convergence ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"), on the other hand, applies to Markov and general extensive form games.
### 1.2 Article outline
---
We would like to prove an analogous result to Theorem [5.4](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S5.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 5.4. ‣ 5.1 Asymptotic convergence of SM-MCTS-A ‣ 5 Convergence of SM-MCTS and SM-MCTS-A ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games") for SM-MCTS. Unfortunately, such a goal is unattainable in general – in Section [4](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S4 "4 Insufficiency of Local Regret Minimization for Global Convergence ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games") we presented a counterexample, showing that a such a theorem with no additional assumptions does not hold.
We show that if an ϵ\\epsilon-HC algorithm with guaranteed exploration has an additional property of ‘having ϵ\\epsilon-unbiased payoff observations’ (ϵ\\epsilon-UPO, see Definition [5.11](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S5.Thmtheorem11 "Definition 5.11 (UPO). ‣ 5.2.1 Definition of the UPO property ‣ 5.2 Asymptotic convergence of SM-MCTS ‣ 5 Convergence of SM-MCTS and SM-MCTS-A ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games")), it can be used as a selection policy for SM-MCTS, and it will always find an approximate equilibrium (Theorem [5.12](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S5.Thmtheorem12 "Theorem 5.12. ‣ 5.2.2 The convergence of SM-MCTS ‣ 5.2 Asymptotic convergence of SM-MCTS ‣ 5 Convergence of SM-MCTS and SM-MCTS-A ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games")). While we were unable to prove that specific ϵ\\epsilon-HC algorithms have the ϵ\\epsilon-UPO property, in Section [7](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S7 "7 Experimental evaluation ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"), we provide empirical evidence supporting our hypothesis that the ‘typical’ algorithms, such as regret matching or Exp3, indeed do have ϵ\\epsilon-unbiased payoff observations.

In Section [2](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S2 "2 Background ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games") we describe simultaneous-move games, the standard class of SM-MCTS algorithms, and our modification SM-MCTS-A. We then describe the multi-armed bandit problem, the definition of Hannan consistency, and explain two of the common Hannan consistent bandit algorithms (Exp3 and regret matching).
We also explain the relation of the studied problem with counterfactual regret minimization, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and shortest path problems.
In Section [3](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S3 "3 Application of the MAB Problem to SM-MCTS(-A) ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"), we explain the relation of SM-MCTS setting with the multi-armed bandit problem. In this section, we also define the technical notation which is used in the proofs of our main results.
In Section [4](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S4 "4 Insufficiency of Local Regret Minimization for Global Convergence ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"), we provide a counterexample showing that for general Hannan consistent algorithms, SM-MCTS does not necessarily converge. While interesting in itself, this result also hints at which modifications are sufficient to get convergence.
The positive theoretical results are presented in Section [5](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S5 "5 Convergence of SM-MCTS and SM-MCTS-A ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"). First, we consider the modified SM-MCTS-A and present the asymptotic bound on its convergence rate.
We follow by defining the unbiased payoff observations property and proving the convergence of SM-MCTS based on HC selection policies with this property. We then present an example which gives a lower bound on the quality of a strategy to which SM-MCTS(-A) converges.
In Section [6](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S6 "6 Exploitability and exploration removal ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"), we make a few remarks about which strategy should be considered as the output of SM-MCTS(-A).
In Section [7](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S7 "7 Experimental evaluation ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games"), we present an empirical investigation of convergence of SM-MCTS and SM-MCTS-A, as well as empirical evidence supporting that the commonly used HC-algorithms guarantee the UPO property. Finally, Section [8](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#S8 "8 Conclusion ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games") summarizes the results and highlights open questions which might be interesting for future research.
Table [2](https://arxiv.org/html/1804.09045#Sx1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Acknowledgements ‣ Analysis of Hannan Consistent Selection for Monte CarloTree Search in Simultaneous Move Games") then recapitulates the notation and abbreviations used throughout the paper.
## 2 Background

We now introduce the game theory fundamentals and notation used throughout the paper. We define simultaneous-move games, describe
the class of SM-MCTS algorithms and its modification SM-MCTS-A, and afterward, we discuss existing selection policies and their properties.
### 2.1 Simultaneous move games

A finite two-player zero-sum game with perfect information and simultaneous moves
can be described by a tuple G=(ℋ,𝒵,𝒜,𝒯,u,h0)G=(\\mathcal{H},\\mathcal{Z},\\mathcal{A},\\mathcal{T},u,h\_{0}),
where ℋ\\mathcal{H} is a set of inner states and 𝒵\\mathcal{Z} denotes the terminal states222
